evidence: Abstract, Secs.I-IV (pp.1-3,7-8): bootstrap stability of Bayesian-AIME vs SHAP and LIME on tabular Titanic, breast-cancer and synthetic data
problem: Most XAI methods give single-point explanations without reliability information, and these explanations change with small data or seed changes.
method: Bayesian extension of approximate inverse model explanations (AIME) with closed-form posterior and credible intervals; bootstrap stability analysis against SHAP and LIME; synthetic validation of interval coverage.
data: Synthetic data with known importance; Titanic survival; breast-cancer diagnosis (p.1).
evaluation: Spearman rank correlation and normalised attribution standard deviation across bootstrap resamples; CI coverage.
findings: Kept mean Spearman rank correlation (0.969), improved explanation stability by 7% and reduced normalised attribution SD by 58% compared with SHAP and LIME (p.2).
limitations: Ours: SHAP/LIME only as comparators; stability under bootstrap resampling, not input perturbation.
repro: Author repository https://github.com/ntakafumi/aime explicitly lists BayesianAIME on 6 November 2026; repository contents and reproduction of this paper were not tested. This is an audit-date availability update, not evidence of availability at the original search date.
qa_notes: Q3 dataset sizes not checked; Q7 method limitations only; Q8 original score retained provisionally; author repository located on audit date, reproducibility not tested; Q10 50 bootstrap resamples.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.I and III.E (pp.1,3-4,8): SHAP explainability stability (E) reported as a separate score across perturbed synthetic clinical worlds (borderline)
problem: Clinical ML benchmarks rarely quantify how SHAP attributions deform under noise, shift and surrogate drift.
method: Seven synthetic clinical 'worlds' (noise, missingness, outliers, shift, surrogate drift, label noise); linear, tree, kernel, neural and ensemble models over 15,000+ configurations; integrity profile R, S, C, E combined into an RSCE index.
data: Synthetic clinical cohort; MIMIC-IV mortality used for external alignment (pp.6,19).
evaluation: E score from global-importance rank correlation, local SHAP cosine similarity and normalised Wasserstein distance between reference and perturbed worlds; Spearman/Kendall with bootstrap CIs and permutation p-values (p.18).
findings: Correlations between synthetic RSCE and real-world degradation were modest and uncertain because few models were evaluated (p.18).
limitations: Authors: small number of evaluated models for external validation (p.18). Ours: stability is one of four dimensions; perturbations change predictions.
qa_notes: Q9 clinical data use without ethics detail in sections read; Q10 configurations and bootstrap CIs.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.III-IV (pp.1-2,5-11): LIME vs H-LIME stability (Jaccard, Spearman over 10 perturbation runs) on two tabular educational datasets
problem: LIME's operating limits on large, high-dimensional behavioural data are unverified.
method: Benchmark of hierarchical LIME (H-LIME) vs LIME with logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost; 10 x 10 repeated cross-validation; probability calibration; 10 independent perturbation runs per instance.
data: Kaggle online-learning adaptability dataset (1,205 instances; mostly categorical) and OULAD behavioural logs (p.5).
evaluation: Jaccard similarity and Spearman correlation across perturbation runs; Kruskal-Wallis tests for subgroup attributions (p.11).
findings: LIME was stable on the socio-economic dataset (rho about 0.87) but collapsed on the high-dimensional behavioural dataset (rho about 0.35); H-LIME mitigated the instability (abstract).
limitations: Ours: significance argued from non-overlapping SD-based intervals; education domain only.
qa_notes: Q6 inference from SD intervals; Q8 not verified; Q9 student data, ethics not seen; Q10 repeated runs.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.III-V (pp.1-2,4-5,13-14): generalisability, concordance and stability of SHAP and LIME combined with k-fold on tabular hypothyroidism and diabetes data
problem: Explanations can vary considerably for similar instances and across data samples, undermining reliability in healthcare.
method: SHAP and LIME computed within k-fold cross-validation for several k; random forest; Spearman similarity of feature-rank lists across k (generalisability), concordance with internal RF importance, and a stability metric.
evaluation: Spearman correlation of rankings across k values; concordance; stability.
findings: SHAP with k-fold showed higher generalisability, stability and concordance than LIME; LIME showed poor concordance and reliability (pp.13-14).
limitations: Ours: two medical datasets; one model; variation from resampling, not input perturbation.
qa_notes: Q3 dataset sizes not checked; Q6 two case studies; Q8 not verified; Q9 health data; Q10 multiple k values.
